title: Kubernetes Essentials
scopeHtml:
Scope: what Kubernetes does, pods/Deployments/Services, probes, resources and autoscaling, config and secrets, debugging rollouts.

Scope: scheduling, networking and policy, Ingress and TLS, RBAC, workload types, service mesh.

notes.title: What Kubernetes does
notes.html:
Running one container is easy; running 500 across 40 machines is not. Kubernetes (K8s) is an orchestrator: you declare the desired state ("run 5 copies of this image, reachable at this address") and its control loops keep making reality match it. A machine dies? It restarts the pods elsewhere. Traffic rises? It can add copies.

Architecture: the control plane (API server, etcd storing state, scheduler choosing a node for each pod, controller manager running the reconcile loops) and worker nodes (kubelet agent, container runtime, kube-proxy for networking).

Worked example. You declare replicas: 3. One node loses power, taking 1 pod. The ReplicaSet controller sees 2 ≠ 3 and the scheduler creates a new pod on a healthy node, with no human involved, typically within a minute.

Industry examples. Kubernetes grew out of Google's internal Borg; Spotify, Airbnb, Pinterest and OpenAI run large clusters; most teams use managed ones (EKS, GKE, AKS) so they do not operate the control plane.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant manager with a staffing sheet: "always 5 waiters on the floor". Someone leaves, the manager calls in a replacement without being told.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Kubernetes "runs containers". The kubelet's runtime runs them; Kubernetes schedules and heals them.
  • Forgetting pods are disposable: IPs and names change.

notes.title: Pods, Deployments and Services
notes.html:
• Pod: the smallest unit; one or more containers sharing network and storage. Pods are ephemeral.
  • Deployment: manages a ReplicaSet of identical pods and does rolling updates and rollbacks.
  • Service: a stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of changing pods, selecting them by labels; kube-proxy load-balances.
  • Ingress (or Gateway API): routes external HTTP(S) by host/path to Services, terminates TLS.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: api }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: { maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 }   # never drop below 3 ready
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: api } }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/api:9f2c1ab        # immutable tag
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }   # scheduler uses this
            limits:   { memory: 512Mi }
          readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 5 }
          livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /live,  port: 8080 }, initialDelaySeconds: 20 }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: api }
spec:
  selector: { app: api }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]

Industry examples. Ingress controllers such as NGINX, Traefik, Envoy-based Gateways front most clusters.

Everyday analogy. Pods are temp workers who come and go; the Service is the company's phone number that always reaches whoever is on shift.

Common interview traps.

  • Pointing at a pod IP instead of a Service.
  • Putting stateful data in a Deployment pod's disk (use StatefulSet + PersistentVolume or a managed DB).

notes.title: Probes, resources and autoscaling
notes.html:
Probes tell Kubernetes about health:

  • Readiness: "send me traffic?" Fail → removed from the Service but not restarted. Crucial during rolling updates.
  • Liveness: "am I stuck?" Fail → container restarted.
  • Startup: gives slow-starting apps time before liveness begins.

Requests are what the scheduler reserves; limits are the cap. Exceeding the memory limit gets the container OOMKilled; exceeding the CPU limit only throttles it.

HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) adds/removes pods based on CPU, memory or custom metrics; VPA adjusts requests; Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter adds nodes when pods cannot be placed. PodDisruptionBudget guarantees a minimum of pods stay up during node drains.

Worked example. Target CPU 70%, 4 pods at 140% of their request each: desired = ceil(4 × 140 / 70) = 8 pods. HPA scales to 8 within its sync interval (about 15 s) bounded by min/max.

Industry examples. Black Friday traffic at e-commerce companies scales HPA plus node autoscaling; Uber and Zalando tune requests carefully because over-requesting wastes cloud money.

Everyday analogy. Readiness is the "open/closed" sign on a shop door; liveness is the manager checking the shopkeeper is still conscious.

Common interview traps.

  • Liveness probe that checks the database: a DB blip restarts every pod, creating a cascading outage.
  • No requests set: the scheduler overpacks nodes.
  • Memory limit lower than the JVM heap plus overhead: constant OOMKills.

notes.title: Config, Secrets and storage
notes.html:
• ConfigMap: non-sensitive config as env vars or mounted files. Secret: base64-encoded (not encrypted by default!) sensitive data; enable encryption at rest and use RBAC, or better an external store (External Secrets Operator, Vault, cloud secret managers).
  • Namespaces divide a cluster by team/environment; RBAC controls who can do what.
  • PersistentVolume/PersistentVolumeClaim give pods durable disks; StatefulSet gives stable identity and storage for databases and Kafka.
  • Helm packages manifests as templated charts with a values file per environment; Kustomize patches base manifests per environment without templates.
helm upgrade --install api ./chart -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=9f2c1ab --atomic

--atomic rolls back automatically if the release fails.

Industry examples. Most teams keep one chart and values-dev/stage/prod.yaml; Argo CD and Flux deploy those charts (see GitOps).

Everyday analogy. A ConfigMap is the notice board; a Secret is the locked key cabinet.

Common interview traps.

  • "Secrets are encrypted": by default they are only base64.
  • Committing a values file with real passwords.

notes.title: Debugging a Kubernetes rollout
notes.html:
Common failures and the command that reveals them:

Symptom Likely cause First command
ImagePullBackOff wrong tag, no registry credentials kubectl describe pod
CrashLoopBackOff app exits on start (bad config, missing env) kubectl logs --previous
Pending no node has enough CPU/memory, taint, PVC not bound kubectl describe pod (Events)
OOMKilled memory limit too low or leak kubectl describe pod (Last State)
Running but no traffic failing readiness probe or wrong Service selector kubectl get endpoints 
kubectl rollout status deploy/api
kubectl rollout undo deploy/api        # one-command rollback to previous ReplicaSet
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

Industry examples. Many outages are config, not code: a typo in an Ingress or a missing ConfigMap key; that is why teams validate manifests in CI (kubeconform, OPA/Kyverno policies) before applying.

Everyday analogy. A hospital triage chart: read the symptom, check the matching vital sign.

Common interview traps.

  • Restarting pods repeatedly instead of reading logs and events.
  • Not knowing --previous for crashed containers.

notes.title: Scheduling: where pods land
notes.html:
The scheduler filters nodes that can run a pod (enough requested CPU/memory, matching selectors, tolerated taints) and then scores the rest. You influence it with:

  • nodeSelector / node affinity: run on nodes with a label (gpu=true, zone=ap-south-1a).
  • Pod affinity / anti-affinity: co-locate or spread pods ("never put two replicas on the same node").
  • Taints and tolerations: a taint repels pods unless they tolerate it (dedicated nodes, spot nodes).
  • Topology spread constraints: spread replicas evenly across zones.
  • PriorityClass: important pods can preempt less important ones.
topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1
    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
    whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
    labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }

Worked example. 3 replicas all land in one zone; the zone fails and the service is down. Spreading across 3 zones keeps 2 of 3 replicas alive.

Industry examples. Cost-focused teams run stateless workloads on spot instances with tolerations and PodDisruptionBudgets; ML teams use taints to reserve GPU nodes.

Everyday analogy. Seating guests at a wedding: separate the feuding relatives (anti-affinity), keep the family together (affinity), and reserve the VIP table (taints).

Common interview traps.

  • High availability claimed with all replicas on one node or one zone.
  • A pod Pending forever because of requests larger than any node.

notes.title: Networking: CNI, DNS and NetworkPolicy
notes.html:
Every pod gets its own IP via a CNI plugin and can reach any other pod by default. CoreDNS gives Services names like orders.shop.svc.cluster.local. kube-proxy (iptables/IPVS) or eBPF dataplanes (Cilium) implement Service load balancing.

By default the cluster network is fully open. NetworkPolicy restricts it: a typical pattern is default-deny and then allow only needed paths (frontend → API → database).

kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: db-only-from-api }
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: db } }
  ingress:
    - from: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api } } }]
      ports: [{ port: 5432 }]

Policies need a CNI that enforces them (Calico, Cilium).

Industry examples. Regulated companies enforce default-deny namespaces; Cilium adds identity-aware and L7 policies.

Everyday analogy. An office where, by default, every door is open; policy is the badge reader that limits who can enter which room.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing namespaces isolate network traffic. They do not, without NetworkPolicy.
  • DNS issues (ndots, CoreDNS overload) causing slow or failing lookups at scale.

notes.title: Ingress, Gateway API and TLS
notes.html:
An Ingress (or the newer Gateway API) routes external HTTP(S) to Services by host and path, handled by a controller (NGINX, Traefik, Envoy/Istio gateway, cloud load balancers). TLS certificates are issued and renewed automatically by cert-manager with Let's Encrypt. A Service of type LoadBalancer provisions one cloud load balancer per service, which is costly; an Ingress shares one.

kind: Ingress
spec:
  tls: [{ hosts: [api.acme.com], secretName: api-tls }]
  rules:
    - host: api.acme.com
      http: { paths: [{ path: /, pathType: Prefix,
              backend: { service: { name: api, port: { number: 80 } } } }] }

Set timeouts, body-size limits and rate limits at the edge; enable HTTP/2 and compression where useful.

Industry examples. Many companies put a CDN/WAF (Cloudflare, CloudFront) in front of the Ingress; Gateway API is replacing Ingress-specific annotations.

Everyday analogy. The building's reception desk: it checks who you want to see and sends you to the right floor.

Common interview traps.

  • Expired TLS certificates because renewal was manual.
  • One LoadBalancer per service, multiplying cost.

notes.title: RBAC, namespaces and multi-tenancy
notes.html:
Namespaces group resources and scope names, quotas and policies. RBAC (Roles, ClusterRoles, bindings) controls who can do which verbs on which resources; ServiceAccounts are identities for pods. Principle of least privilege: developers read logs in their namespace, only CI/GitOps tooling changes production, nobody uses cluster-admin day to day.

Add ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges so one team cannot consume the whole cluster, and Pod Security Standards (restricted profile) to block privileged pods.

Worked example. A pod's default ServiceAccount token can list secrets because someone bound it to cluster-admin "temporarily". A compromised pod then reads every secret in the cluster.

Industry examples. Platform teams give each squad a namespace with quotas, network policy and a pre-wired GitOps Application; cloud providers map IAM roles to ServiceAccounts (IRSA, Workload Identity).

Everyday analogy. Office key cards: staff open their own floor, only facilities opens the server room.

Common interview traps.

  • Binding cluster-admin to CI for convenience.
  • Treating namespaces as a hard security boundary on their own.

notes.title: Jobs, CronJobs, DaemonSets and StatefulSets
notes.html:
Beyond Deployments:

  • Job: run to completion (a migration, a batch import), with retries (backoffLimit).
  • CronJob: a Job on a schedule; set concurrencyPolicy (Forbid/Replace) so runs do not pile up.
  • DaemonSet: one pod per node (log shippers, node agents).
  • StatefulSet: stable pod names (db-0), ordered start, a PersistentVolume per replica (databases, Kafka, Elasticsearch).
  • Init containers run before the main container (wait for a dependency, run migrations carefully).

Operators encode operational knowledge (backups, failover, upgrades) for stateful software using custom resources, for example the Postgres, Kafka or Prometheus operators.

Worked example. A nightly report CronJob that takes 70 minutes on a 60-minute schedule starts overlapping itself; concurrencyPolicy: Forbid plus an alert on missed runs fixes it.

Industry examples. Prometheus node-exporter and Fluent Bit run as DaemonSets on every node of most clusters.

Everyday analogy. Deployment = shop staff (interchangeable); StatefulSet = named lockers each with its own key; DaemonSet = a security guard on every floor.

Common interview traps.

  • Running migrations as init containers on every replica concurrently.
  • Treating StatefulSets as a complete database solution without backups and failover.

notes.title: Service mesh and where it fits
notes.html:
A service mesh (Istio, Linkerd, Cilium service mesh) adds a proxy (sidecar or per-node) to every pod to provide mTLS between services, retries and timeouts, traffic splitting (canary by percentage), and rich telemetry without changing application code.

Costs: extra CPU and memory per pod, more moving parts, harder debugging and upgrades. Many teams delay a mesh until they truly need zero-trust mTLS or fine-grained traffic control; simpler libraries or an ingress with weighted routing may suffice.

Worked example. Istio VirtualService sends 5% of traffic to v2 and 95% to v1, giving a canary without touching either application.

Industry examples. Lyft created Envoy; Google, eBay and Airbnb run Istio at scale; Linkerd is a lighter alternative.

Everyday analogy. A personal assistant for each employee who handles calls, checks IDs and logs conversations so employees can focus on work.

Common interview traps.

  • Adopting a mesh "because everyone does" with no clear problem.
  • Forgetting the latency and resource overhead of sidecars.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html: Kubernetes keeps declared desired state true with reconcile loops: control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controllers) plus nodes running kubelet. Pods are ephemeral; Deployments handle rolling updates and rollbacks; Services give stable access; Ingress handles external HTTP. Use readiness, liveness and startup probes correctly, set resource requests and limits, and scale with HPA, Cluster Autoscaler and PodDisruptionBudgets. Treat Secrets carefully (base64 is not encryption), package with Helm or Kustomize, and debug with describe, logs --previous, events and rollout undo.

questions.promptHtml: What problem does Kubernetes solve, and what are its main components?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A baseline for any backend or DevOps role.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It runs and manages containers across many machines. You declare the desired state, such as five replicas of an image, and controllers continuously make reality match it, restarting failed pods and rescheduling them. Control plane: API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager. Each node runs kubelet, a container runtime and kube-proxy.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Everything goes through the API server, which stores state in etcd. The scheduler picks a node for each unscheduled pod based on resource requests, taints and affinity. Controllers reconcile: a ReplicaSet controller notices 2 pods when 3 are desired and creates one. This declarative, level-triggered design makes the system self-healing.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying Kubernetes itself runs containers (the container runtime does).
  • Treating pod IPs as stable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if etcd is lost? → The cluster state is gone; back up etcd regularly (or use managed control planes).
  2. Why use managed Kubernetes? → Offloads control plane operation and upgrades.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior explains the reconcile loop and failure modes of the control plane.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between a Pod, a Deployment and a Service?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Verifies you know the core objects and why a Service is needed.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Pod is the smallest unit, one or more containers sharing network and storage, and it is disposable. A Deployment manages replicas of identical pods and handles rolling updates and rollbacks. A Service gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name that load-balances to whichever pods match its label selector.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Pods get new IPs when recreated, so clients cannot depend on them. The Service selects pods by labels and the endpoints list updates as pods become ready or not. Ingress or Gateway API routes external HTTP traffic to Services and terminates TLS.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrong label selector, so the Service has no endpoints.
  • Running a bare Pod instead of a Deployment (no self-healing).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Service types? → ClusterIP (internal), NodePort, LoadBalancer.
  2. StatefulSet vs Deployment? → Stable identity and storage for stateful workloads.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior knows the endpoints/readiness link and when to use StatefulSets or operators.

questions.promptHtml: Explain readiness, liveness and startup probes. What goes wrong if you configure them badly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Misconfigured probes cause real outages.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Readiness decides whether a pod receives traffic; failing it removes the pod from the Service without restarting. Liveness decides whether the container is stuck; failing it restarts the container. Startup gives slow-starting apps time before liveness begins. A liveness probe that checks a dependency like the database can restart every pod during a DB blip and turn a small problem into a full outage.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Rolling updates rely on readiness: a new pod must be ready before an old one is stopped. Too-aggressive liveness (short timeout, low failure threshold) kills busy-but-healthy pods under load, shedding capacity and worsening the load (a death spiral). Liveness should test only the process itself.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Same endpoint and thresholds for readiness and liveness.
  • No startup probe for a JVM app that takes 60 seconds to boot.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does graceful shutdown need? → Handle SIGTERM, drain, preStop and a termination grace period.
  2. What if readiness always returns OK? → Traffic hits unready pods, causing errors.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior explains cascading failure risk and tuning from real startup metrics.

questions.promptHtml: What are resource requests and limits, and how does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler decide to scale?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cost and reliability both depend on this.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Requests are what the scheduler reserves for a pod; limits are the maximum. Exceeding the memory limit kills the container (OOMKilled); exceeding the CPU limit only throttles it. HPA computes desired replicas as ceil(current × currentMetric / targetMetric), bounded by min and max, using CPU, memory or custom metrics.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: No requests means the scheduler overpacks nodes, causing noisy-neighbour problems. Requests too high wastes money. HPA needs requests set to compute utilisation percentages. Pair HPA with Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter so there are nodes to place new pods, and use PodDisruptionBudgets to protect availability during node drains.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• JVM heap near the memory limit leaving no room for non-heap memory (OOMKilled).
  • HPA scaling on CPU for an I/O-bound service.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. 4 pods at 140% of target 70%? → ceil(4 × 140/70) = 8.
  2. Why CPU limits are debated? → Throttling can hurt latency; many teams set requests only.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions custom/queue-based metrics, scale-down stabilisation and right-sizing with VPA data.

questions.promptHtml: Are Kubernetes Secrets secure? How do you manage secrets properly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A common misconception.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: By default Secrets are only base64-encoded, not encrypted, and anyone with API read access to them can decode them. Enable encryption at rest, restrict access with RBAC, and ideally keep real secrets in an external manager (Vault, AWS or GCP Secret Manager) synced by the External Secrets Operator or a CSI driver. For GitOps use Sealed Secrets or SOPS so nothing plain lives in Git.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Secrets mounted as files update over time, env vars do not until restart. Prefer workload identity (IAM roles for service accounts) over static cloud keys. Rotate regularly. Audit who can get secrets.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Committing base64 secrets to Git.
  • Giving developers broad namespace-wide secret read access.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. ConfigMap vs Secret? → Non-sensitive vs sensitive data; neither is encrypted by default.
  2. How does a pod pick up new config? → Mounted files refresh; env vars need a rollout.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior designs rotation, workload identity and audit trails.

questions.contextHtml: You deploy a new image to production. kubectl get pods shows the new pods in CrashLoopBackOff with 6 restarts, while the 3 old pods are still serving traffic. The old ReplicaSet is not being scaled down. Users are unaffected so far. Logs from the current container are empty.
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through diagnosing and resolving this.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Deletes pods repeatedly, hoping they recover.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed (image, config, secrets, env vars)? Did staging pass? Is this a probe failure or a process exit?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Nothing user-facing is broken because rolling update keeps old pods; I would pause or kubectl rollout undo if the situation changes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Missing or wrong config/secret; app crashes at startup; OOMKilled; failing liveness probe; bad entrypoint.
  4. How I'd verify: kubectl logs <pod> --previous, kubectl describe pod (Last State, exit code, Events), kubectl get events.
  5. Root cause: Typical case: a required environment variable absent from the production ConfigMap, so the app exits with code 1.
  6. Fix: Add the missing config through the normal GitOps path, redeploy; roll forward or undo.
  7. Prevention: Validate config on startup with a clear error, validate manifests in CI, test in staging with prod-like config, set progressDeadlineSeconds so rollouts fail loudly.
  8. Trade-offs: rollout undo is fastest but does not fix the cause; fixing forward needs a new commit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Exit code 137? → Killed (often OOM); check memory limit and heap.
  • Pods stuck Pending? → Insufficient resources, taints or unbound PVC; see Events.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rollout was "green" for hours because readiness always returned OK; the real fix was a readiness check that exercised the app's main dependency path.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts randomly.
  • Hire: --previous logs, describe, events, undo.
  • Strong hire: explains why users were protected, adds prevention.

questions.promptHtml: Three replicas of your service all land in the same availability zone. How do you make them highly available?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: HA claims without spreading are a classic mistake.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use topology spread constraints (or pod anti-affinity) so replicas spread across zones and nodes, together with a PodDisruptionBudget. Taints and tolerations and node affinity control which nodes pods may use; PriorityClass decides who is preempted when resources are tight.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The scheduler filters nodes by requests, selectors and taints, then scores the rest. maxSkew: 1 across topology.kubernetes.io/zone keeps replicas even. Requests larger than any node leave pods Pending forever.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling it HA with all replicas on one node or zone.
  • Hard anti-affinity with too few nodes, leaving pods unschedulable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Spot instances? → Tolerations and enough on-demand capacity plus PDBs.
  2. Why Pending? → kubectl describe pod Events.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior balances spread, cost and disruption budgets.

questions.promptHtml: Are Kubernetes namespaces a network security boundary? How do you restrict traffic?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A frequent false assumption.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: No. By default every pod can reach every other pod across namespaces. Use NetworkPolicies: start with default-deny and allow only required paths, for example frontend to API to database. Policies only work if the CNI enforces them (Calico, Cilium).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: CoreDNS resolves service names; kube-proxy or eBPF implements Service load balancing. Cilium adds identity-aware and L7 policy. DNS issues (ndots, overloaded CoreDNS) cause slow lookups at scale.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing policies on a CNI that does not enforce them.
  • Forgetting to allow DNS egress after default-deny.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Egress control? → Egress policies or gateways.
  2. mTLS? → Service mesh or Cilium.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior designs default-deny rollout and observes flows first.

questions.promptHtml: How does external traffic reach a service in Kubernetes, and how are TLS certificates managed?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every production service needs it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An Ingress or Gateway API resource, implemented by a controller (NGINX, Traefik, Envoy, cloud load balancer), routes external HTTP(S) by host and path to Services and terminates TLS. cert-manager issues and renews certificates automatically, for example from Let's Encrypt, so they do not expire.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: One shared Ingress avoids one cloud LoadBalancer per Service, which is expensive. Set timeouts, body-size limits and rate limits at the edge. A CDN or WAF often sits in front.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Manual certificate renewal leading to expiry outages.
  • One LoadBalancer Service per app.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Gateway API vs Ingress? → More expressive and role-oriented, replacing annotation sprawl.
  2. mTLS inside the cluster? → Service mesh.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior adds certificate monitoring and edge protections.

questions.promptHtml: How do you give a CI system or developers appropriate access to a cluster?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Over-privileged access is a classic incident cause.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Least privilege with RBAC: Roles and RoleBindings scoped to a namespace, ServiceAccounts for pods and tooling, no day-to-day cluster-admin. In a GitOps setup only the GitOps controller changes production and developers get read access. Add ResourceQuotas, LimitRanges and Pod Security Standards for multi-tenancy.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Map cloud IAM roles to ServiceAccounts (IRSA, Workload Identity) rather than using static keys. A pod with an over-privileged ServiceAccount token can read every secret if compromised.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Binding cluster-admin to CI "temporarily".
  • Assuming namespaces alone isolate tenants.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you audit? → Audit logs and tools like kubectl auth can-i, rbac-lookup.
  2. Break-glass access? → Time-limited, logged elevation.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior designs break-glass, quotas and workload identity.

questions.promptHtml: When would you use a Job, CronJob, DaemonSet and StatefulSet instead of a Deployment?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows breadth beyond stateless web apps.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Job for run-to-completion work like a data migration; CronJob for scheduled Jobs with concurrencyPolicy to prevent overlap; DaemonSet for one pod per node such as log shippers; StatefulSet for stable identity and per-pod persistent storage, as in databases or Kafka.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Operators encode operational knowledge (backups, failover) for stateful software. Init containers run before the main container; migrations in init containers run on every replica unless guarded.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• CronJob runs overlapping because it takes longer than its interval.
  • Running a database in a StatefulSet without backups or failover.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Job failed halfway? → backoffLimit, make it idempotent.
  2. Where do migrations belong? → A dedicated Job or pipeline step, run once.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior prefers managed databases or mature operators.

questions.promptHtml: What does a service mesh provide and when would you not adopt one?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests judgement about complexity.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A mesh (Istio, Linkerd, Cilium) adds a proxy per pod or node giving mTLS between services, retries and timeouts, traffic splitting for canaries, and uniform telemetry without app changes. The cost is extra CPU and memory, operational complexity and harder debugging, so I would adopt it only for a clear need such as zero-trust mTLS or fine-grained traffic control.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Sidecar overhead adds latency and resources per pod; sidecar-less ambient modes reduce it. Alternatives: ingress weighted routing, client libraries, or network policy.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adopting a mesh because it is popular.
  • Ignoring upgrade and debugging burden.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does it help canaries? → Percentage-based routing.
  2. What is Envoy? → The proxy used by Istio and many gateways.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior justifies the trade-off and plans operations.

questions.contextHtml: During a traffic spike the HPA scales a Deployment from 6 to 20 replicas, but 9 new pods stay Pending. Latency climbs and error rate hits 3%. kubectl describe pod says "0/12 nodes are available: insufficient cpu". Cluster Autoscaler is installed but no new nodes appear.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Manually restarts pods or raises the HPA max.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Node group max size? Autoscaler logs? Pod requests? Any quotas or instance-type limits in the cloud account?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Manually scale the node group or shed load (rate-limit non-critical traffic), and preempt low-priority workloads with PriorityClass.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Node group at its max size; cloud quota reached; pods request more than any node offers; autoscaler misconfigured or unable to pick a node group (labels/taints).
  4. How I'd verify: Autoscaler logs and events, cloud console quotas, kubectl describe, node group configuration.
  5. Root cause: Typically the node group maximum or an account quota prevents scale-out.
  6. Fix: Raise limits, request quota increases, add node groups or use Karpenter with diverse instance types.
  7. Prevention: Headroom buffer (overprovisioning pods), load-test scaling, alerts on Pending pods, right-size requests.
  8. Trade-offs: Headroom costs money; the buffer is cheaper than an outage.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• New nodes take 4 minutes → use overprovisioning and pre-warmed capacity.
  • HPA and cluster limit conflict → align max replicas with node capacity.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch event stalled because a cloud vCPU quota was hit; teams now check quotas as part of launch readiness.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts pods.
  • Hire: reads Events, finds autoscaler limits.
  • Strong hire: quotas, headroom and launch readiness.
